I'm starting college in about a month and would like to see what advice the community of Voat can give me.

Edit: I forgot to add I'm going to be staying on campus.
Any advice to give to a incoming freshman? (4 year university)
Drink less, pay attention more. Now that I'm a big kid I wish more than anything I could just go back to sit and hear someone speak about their passion for a day.
Keep your door open and you'll meet so many new people and make a lot of friends
Exactly. My group of friends always left the door open while hanging out. We'd usually end up having random karaoke sessions with total strangers popping in just to sing a verse and then leave.

Choose courses based on interest, not ease. Your marks will suffer far more from boredom than difficulty, and you'll regret the wasted time later on. Professors can also smell interest, and they'll go out of their way for you when they see it whether it's fixing a TA screwup, arranging an internship or helping you get into a master's program.

On the flip side, sometimes it'll be worth it to take a class you have absolutely no interest in, just to sort of broaden your horizons. Only if you think you're academically up to it, though, of course.

I took a class that was entirely devoted to a single text by an author I absolutely hated.

Now it's, like, the book that defines me as a person.
Find someone who wants to be a doctor and marry them.

Get to know the people on your hall, you never know when you'll need them to save the day. Befriend your RA, you'll be surprised with what you can get away with by doing that. Befriend your roommates and classmates as well. Go through rush, it's a great way to meet people even if you don't pledge. Join a club. Go to class. Read your textbooks, do your homework, and do NOT party every night.

Get out and about. Yes college is about learning, but it's also about social development. You will NEVER again have access to this many people with such common ground. You'll never find friends and relationships easier than you will in college.

Follow your passions. Find clubs for your interest and join them. If you hate your major, change it. If you're in the wrong major the sooner you change it, the easier.

Do what you can to minimize your debt. Don't go blowing your student loan dispersal on toys (whatever flavor your toys may take). At the same time, though, remember that you're there for school; getting a little deeper in debt is preferable to dropping out so you can get a few more hours at the Stop & Rob.

Make use of your professors office hours. Talk to all of them at least once. Remember that they're humans just like you. Some of them will be terrible wastes of oxygen, some will make great friends. Professors are typically more lenient with students that come in and talk to them than names they only know from scoring tests.

Talk to your advisor. Get their advice before you take a bunch of classes that don't work for your major.

READ THE GODDAMN SYLLABUS. Don't be that toolbag that asks questions that are answered by the syllabus. The syllabus is your contract, and knowing it can save your ass.

This one can be a gamble, but at the school I went to, Professors had to list a book for the class, even if they didn't use one. Sometimes they'd list a number of books that were nothing more than recommended reading. I found that not buying my books until after the first class saved me hundreds of dollars per semester.
So much good advice in one comment.

Feedback from a recent graduate:

You will NEVER again have access to this many people with such common ground. You'll never find friends and relationships easier than you will in college.

This SO fucking hard. I just graduated in June, and I'm one of the lucky ones who found a good job right away. There's probably about three people in the entire company my age, and none of them are particularly sociable, interesting, or, let's face it, attractive. Neighborhood singles volleyball league, here I come.

Find clubs for your interest and join them.

Or even start them! If you participate in club leadership, they're great resume boosters in terms of event planning, participation in committees, fundraising, political activism, whatever. Find something your passionate in and even if it's not your major, sometimes it'll be enough to land a career in it.

Make use of your professors office hours.

Everyone always says this, and now that I graduated, I really regret not doing it. Some of those men and women are the brightest on the planet. Having a professor for a friend enriches you in so many ways.

READ THE GODDAMN SYLLABUS

Academia's version of RTFM. Seriously, unless the professor's just all over the place, any question you could possibly have on the first day will be answered on the syllabus.

I found that not buying my books until after the first class saved me hundreds of dollars per semester.

Chiming in on that. I took a major that had at least 3 different texts listed as required per course. In my four years, I bought two - one after the last day of class, just so I could see what all the fuss was about.

I think there's a big part of the first point of being social that's being left out here... networking. (Social networking, not computers.) Many, many well off people wouldn't be where they were without the connections they made in college.

If you ever feel like you need a break from the dorms / your roommate / people in general. Find a quiet spot in a back corner of the library, even if you don't have any work to do and just want to dick about on the internet. Sometimes it's nice to just have some time to yourself and that can be hard to find while living in the dorms.
Start your homework once it's assigned. Make life friends who make good choices.
Don't put anything off and don't take assignments/homework too lightly. I didn't take my first year too seriously and payed for it.

what the fuck did you enroll in school for? just educate yourself on the internet. if you really plan on doing something with yoursefl you'll be motivated enough to do it.

plus, the online schools (reputable ones only, for obvious reasons) are better formatted in most ways. just make sure to bridge the social gap. socializing with people in my field is the only useful thing I've gotten from college. Sure I learned stuff but I would have taught myself stuff over the period of time that I went to college.

finish college as soon as you can. don't focus on grades too hard. professors use that as their source of power. confuse them with questions you don't actually have and don't give them any power over you.
If you get a .edu email, get Amazon Prime with it. 6 month free trial of Amazon Student Prime then 50% off Amazon Prime after that. That's about ~$4 a month.

Don't buy the books. I had many classes where the Professor explicitly stated we absolutely needed to purchase a certain version of a textbook only to find out that we never actually used that book for the class. Even if the book is needed you can most certainly find a classmate that will lend you their book for any necessary homework. Plus it gives you the added benefit of meeting new people, if only to borrow their shit.
Dont accept drinks from anyone, pour your own and dont lose sight of it.

Go to class even hungover/still a little drunk. If you don't drink that much all the better. Complete assignments on time, take advantage of office hours amd TAs. I understand this might not be popular, but don't sleep around....it will just mess with your psyche. Don't be afraid to think differently than your peers or professors.
Don't skip class, learn how to skip smarter.

I feel obligated to say this: don't worry or freak out if it doesn't all go exceptionally well immediately. So many people go into university thinking it'll be their one shot at doing the things they never got to do in highschool. I think this is why so many people kill themselves during the first few years, or develop severe mental conditions; they convince themselves beforehand that this is the only chance they'll ever get to be happy, and when it doesn't work out how they want it seems like the end of the world. Try hard socially, but don't be too hard on yourself if you don't find yourself fitting in with what seems like the most popular group in your residence. Take things at your own pace and try not to take it so seriously, people will be attracted to you if you just try to enjoy yourself and understand you're on your own path which can't really be compared to others.

Do NOT go to the bookstore on the first day buying all your books. Go to the class first and unless your final is open book, do not buy the book. See if you can download a pdf online or if you do need the book, get the cheap paperback version from Amazon or AbeBooks

If you are going into engineering make sure your computer has Windows, a lot of the software that I had to use was only available for Windows so the people with Macs had to do all their assignments in the library.

Take notes even if you're never going to use them, you never know when it'll come in handy. It also helps you remember the material and keeps you awake.

Join clubs your first semester/quarter don't wait till later. This way you'll be joining in with a bunch of strangers instead of a club that already has cliques.
